scenario: Finance asks what a new AI workflow will cost. The provider's price list says a fraction of a cent per request.
question: What do you tell them?

options.text: The model bill is real but usually the smallest line. Budget seven lines: model usage, platform, human review, build, maintenance, error cost and data work.
Quote the per-request price multiplied by the expected volume.
Say it is too early to estimate until the workflow is live.

why: In the article's illustrative example, review time and uncaught errors dwarf the model fee. A rough number for each line beats a precise number for only one.

scenario: A workflow reads long email threads, then classifies, extracts, drafts and checks. Your estimate used a short sample ticket.
question: Why is the estimate probably too low?

options.text: Longer inputs, several model calls per task and retries all multiply tokens, so estimates must use realistic median and longest cases.
It is not. The model price per token does not change.
Because output is always cheaper than input.

why: Four calls cost more than one, and a failed step that retries is paid for every time. Estimate with real examples from your own data, not the shortest case.

scenario: Someone proposes switching to a cheaper model to cut the bill. Test results show the error rate would rise a little.
question: How do you judge the trade?

options.text: Re-run the test set and compare total cost, including the error line. A small rise in uncaught errors can cost more than the model savings.
Switch anyway, since cheaper is always better.
Keep the expensive model for everything and never test alternatives.

why: Cost per successful outcome, not cost per run, is the honest measure. Squeezing the model price while the error line is far larger is a poor use of effort.

scenario: A pilot's agent sometimes loops for a long time before finishing. Finance is nervous about bill shock.
question: Which guardrails go in before launch?

options.text: Spending caps with the provider, daily alerts, per-task limits on tokens, steps and time, a separate key per workflow, a kill switch and a named owner.
A monthly reminder to look at the invoice.
Nothing, because free credits cover the first months.

why: Cost control is also about preventing surprises. These controls cost about an hour to set up and make runaway loops visible and stoppable.

scenario: A team plans to run a real workflow on a free plan to save money.
question: What is the sensible approach?

options.text: Use free tiers for testing, write down the limits, set an alert before reaching them and decide the fallback in advance. Check data terms before sending sensitive information.
Run production on it and handle limit problems if they appear.
Send all sensitive data through it since it is only a trial.

why: Free tiers often have low limits, may change without much notice and can have different data terms. They are useful for testing but a poor basis for a budget.
